author: Guardian sport
description:
• West Ham recover from 3-0 down to draw 3-3 at Cardiff

  • Leaders Middlesbrough beaten 2-0 at Wrexham

Scott Parker’s return to West Ham had had looked like beginning in painful fashion but instead featured a stunning comeback from 3-0 down. The east London club’s new head coach had watched Cardiff’s Jack Moylan score a first-half hat-trick, before a rousing response after the break ended with Max Kilman levelling the scores at 3-3 eight minutes from time. Elsewhere in the Championship, the leaders Middlesbrough went down 2-0 at Wrexham.

Parker had been confirmed as West Ham’s head coach earlier on Wednesday, taking over from Nuno Espírito Santo, who was sacked on Tuesday. The club’s former midfielder was appointed on a two-and-a-half-year contract.
title: Championship roundup: West Ham stage dramatic comeback on Scott Parker’s opening night

author: Emma Loffhagen
description:
Alexander: God, King, Man by Edmund Richardson becomes the first ancient history title to win the prestigious nonfiction award

• Alexander: God, King, Man by Edmund Richardson review – a dazzling, dizzying adventure

Edmund Richardson has won the 2026 Baillie Gifford prize for nonfiction for Alexander: God, King, Man, his account of the life of Alexander the Great, becoming the first writer to win the prize for an ancient history book.

Richardson was awarded the £50,000 prize at a ceremony in London on Wednesday evening, beating a six-strong shortlist that included former winner Patrick Radden Keefe’s
title: ‘Blockbuster’ history of Alexander the Great wins £50,000 Baillie Gifford prize

author: Nadeem Badshah
description:
Minister hints at restriction on selling technology ‘to certain users’ amid worries over surreptitious filming of women

Restrictions on smart glasses are being considered by the government, a minister has said, amid concerns that the technology is being used to surreptitiously film women.

Speaking in the House of Commons, the safeguarding minister Satvir Kaur hinted at a ban on selling the technology “to certain users”.

Continue reading...
title: UK government considers smart glasses ban over secret filming concerns

author: AFP
description:
Federico Valverde lashed home a stunning effort from distance to snatch Real Madrid a late 3-2 victory at AEK Athens on Wednesday in the Champions League and preserve their 100% start in the group phase.

José Mourinho’s side twice came from behind against the Greek champions before Valverde claimed all three points for his side.

Continue reading...
title: Valverde’s late winner breaks AEK Athens hearts as Real Madrid twice come from behind

author: Emma Loffhagen
description:
The Rouse, which took its author two decades to complete, was praised by judges as ‘exuberant, overflowing’

China Miéville has won the £10,000 Goldsmiths prize for The Rouse, a 1,264-page epic that is part paranormal thriller, part historical saga moving through decades of British imperial and cold war history.

The win, announced at a ceremony in London on Wednesday, makes The Rouse the longest novel to take the prize since it was launched in 2013 to reward fiction that “breaks the mould or extends the possibilities of the novel form”.

Continue reading...
title: ‘He was destined for this award’: China Miéville wins Goldsmiths prize for 1,200-page novel

author: Presented by Lucy Hough with Ankita Rao ; produced by Angus Neale ; senior producer Leonore Schick ; executive producer Zoe Hitch
description:
Democrats have won a historic sweep in the US midterm elections, winning back control of Congress in a major setback for Donald Trump. Senate seats went blue in traditional Republican strongholds such as Texas, South Carolina and Kansas, where the Democrats had their first win since 1932. Voters have sent a strong message of discontent to the Trump administration over the economy, the cost of living and rising gas prices. Trump is now a lame-duck president for the rest of his term. Lucy Hough speaks to our Washington editor, Ankita Rao

Continue reading...
title: Democrats’ triumph deals devastating blow to Trump - The Latest

author: Editorial
description:
It is getting ever harder for Eurosceptics to deny that it was an economic and strategic blunder for Britain to leave the single market

The EU is a constantly evolving institution. The rules keep changing and, since Britain is destined by geography to want a close economic relationship with the bloc, there will always be something to negotiate in Brussels.

Most of those discussions over the past two years have been uncontroversial, except in the eyes of dogmatic Eurosceptics. That doesn’t mean the talks have been easy. They never are with a club of 27 nations. But later this month, at a summit with the EU commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, Andy Burnham is expected to complete a treaty covering closer cooperation in a wide range of areas, including elimination of customs barriers to agricultural goods, a youth-mobility programme and integrat
title: The Guardian view on EU ‘Made in Europe’ rules: a fatal blow to Brexiter delusions | Editorial

author: John Crace
description:
After his embarrassment of epic proportions, Farage turned up at PMQs – the last place anyone would expect to find him

In what counts as breaking news on this slowest of slow Wednesdays in Westminster – most eyes were on the US midterm elections – it was nice to be able to report that Nigel Farage was in the Commons for prime minister’s questions. Not something you can often say.

Despite Reform UK tanking in the polls, Nige still regards himself as the official opposition and considers it a major insult that he isn’t given six questions every week. Today he was happy not to get one. Not even Nige’s magic shield of narcissism would have been able to save him from hubris. An embarrassment of epic proportions.

The Guardian’s year in review 2026: on Tuesday 1 December, join your favourite Guardian writers for an evening of candid conversations, witty remarks an
title: The pollsters had got it wrong on the US midterms, said Nige. That aged well | John Crace

author: Reuters
description:
• McIlroy: ‘LIV turned pro golf into an arms race’

  • DP chief executive: ‘We pay everyone on time’

Rory McIlroy voiced his support on Wednesday for the DP World Tour chief executive’s claim that LIV Golf’s goal was to “destroy” the European golf circuit.

The six-time major winner and former world No 1 spoke ⁠with the media on Wednesday before the Abu Dhabi Championship and was asked about Guy Kinnings’ recent interview with the Scotsman.

Continue reading...
title: Rory McIlroy backs claim that LIV tried to 'destroy' DP World Tour

author: Greg Wood
description:
The combination of prodigious talent in the saddle and an easy likeability out of it is a perfect fit for Dubai operation

“I want to ride more Group One winners,” Billy Loughnane said last month when asked to name his main ambition for 2027, and Britain’s new 20-year-old champion jockey seems all but certain to achieve his aim, following Wednesday’s news that he has signed a retainer to ride in the royal blue colours of Sheikh Mohammed’s global Godolphin operation next year.

Loughnane will be contracted alongside William Buick as one of two retained Godolphin jockeys next year, and not as an outright No 1, but even if Loughnane does not claim the lion’s share of the best rides as soon as next year, his trajectory within the operation seems clear.

Continue reading...
title: Billy ‘The Kid’ Loughnane can be new ‘face of racing’ and next Dettori after Godolphin deal

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Readers question the motives and fairness behind Shabana Mahmood’s new immigration proposals

This week, the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, announced that many migrants on skilled worker visas earning below £50,000, outside the social care sector, will have to wait for 10 years to “earn” settlement (Shabana Mahmood softens immigration plans in face of cabinet backlash, 2 November). This blatantly overlooks the contribution of those whose work cannot be measured in high salaries.

I arrived in the UK in September 2022 to pursue a master’s degree, for which I paid more than twice the fee that domestic students pay. Since then, I have worked for two organisations, including the Institute of Development Studies, a leading institution for development research. I have paid my taxes and met the financial requirements of successive visas,
title: Why the UK settlement rule changes are unjust | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Such a punitive measure will leave people at risk of exploitation and severe poverty, says Mark Joselin of the Refugee Council

Cabinet ministers are right to be worried about the potential impact of the new asylum bill (Mahmood infuriates fellow ministers by failing to reveal impact of UK migration shake-up, 30 October). The proposed refugee tax unfairly punishes refugees by threatening to slap most with a £10,000 tax once they are granted refugee status, a clear breach of the UN refugee convention.

It is aimed at those who arrived with nothing and were not allowed to work while their claims were being assessed, and it ignores the reality that refugees already contribute through the tax system.
title: The £10,000 refugee tax must be scrapped | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Readers respond to an article by Arwa Mahdawi on some self-catering hosts calling for a strike in response to new guidelines

Regarding Arwa Mahdawi’s article (Airbnb feels like a soulless rip-off – and its hosts are revolting, 28 October), I’m really sick of being scapegoated. I’m aware that Airbnb has negatively impacted some urban communities, but without the income from the two self-catering cottages on my family croft, I couldn’t afford to live in Wester Ross, raise my kids here, spend my money in the village stores and volunteer as a community councillor for the last 25 years.

There may be tyrannical hosts with 90 pages of house rules, but the new guidelines are nonsensical. If self-catering guests are now not expected to wash up, am I supposed to provide them with enough crockery and cutlery for each day of their stay? They’ll then h
title: Airbnb can be positive for the community | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Ed Kelsey and Arthur Gould respond to an interview with the author in which she discussed AI and the future of humanity

I thoroughly enjoyed the interview with Jeanette Winterson (‘There is no inevitable dystopia’: Jeanette Winterson on AI and the future of humanity, 28 October), particularly her quote from Jill Lepore that we are living out the sci-fi books that tech leaders read when they were 13. I was one of those 13-year-olds, and my favourite author was Isaac Asimov.

Many of his stories accurately predicted our modern world, from mobile technology to AI (through his fictional supercomputer Multivac). However, it was Winterson’s closing point – that “of course we will specialise. We need doctors and chemists, but we also need what used to be called well-rounded people” – that really made me smile.
title: Jeanette Winterson’s point about AI brings to mind an Isaac Asimov story | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Forget the French tuck. This year, the fashion press has another style move in mind – and it will at least keep your jeans clean

Name: The knuck.

Age: A brand new term for an enduring look.

Continue reading...
title: The knuck: how to wear trousers and boots – without looking like a pirate

author: Tim Jonze
description:
On day 58, he did a boxing Ali horse. On day 67, he did a howling horse. So what made Andy Field suddenly decide to draw 100 equines? And what made day 48’s turn out so phallic?

Andy Field was midway through his standup run at this year’s Edinburgh fringe when he was struck by an unusual urge – the urge to draw a horse. “I hadn’t sat down to draw anything since I was at school,” says the 34-year-old comedian. “Drawing was a skill I didn’t have.”

He’s not lying. The subsequent horse Field posted to TikTok and Instagram was rather naive, with its four identical straight legs and cartoon eyeball. But the project he announced alongside it – Drawing a Horse Every Day Until I’m Really Good at Drawing Horses – immediately captured people’s hearts. Over a million people watched the minute-long video of him drawing that fi
title: ‘Jimi Horsedrix brought me so much joy’: the comic drawing a horse a day – and day 69’s is unsuitable for children

author: Alice Austin
description:
The cost of checking your coat or bag is galloping ahead of other – also rising – prices at venues. We explain the surprisingly complex reasons why

Not long ago, it cost just £2 to put a coat or a heavily stuffed tote bag in a cloakroom on a night out. But over the course of the 2020s, that cost has increased to more than £13 in some UK venues.

At the Outernet Live venue complex in London’s Soho, it costs £11 to put a bag in a large locker. It’s £9 at east London nightclub Fold, and if you want to retrieve something, you’ll need to pay again. At north London’s Drumsheds, the UK’s biggest nightclub, they cost up to £13.20 (though they’re reusable with no extra fee). At the Warehouse Project in Manchester, large bags must be stored at a nearby Premier Inn at £11.99 per locker. Manchester’s Co-op Live Arena has a dedicated bag storage facility which costs £15 for large bags. It’s £9.99 near the 3,000-capacity Edinburgh Playhouse and £9.90 at Testbed in Leeds. How have doub
title: Once it was a £1 hanger. Now it’s a £15 locker. Why do cloakrooms cost so much on a night out?

author: Robyn Vinter North of England correspondent
description:
Charities say government ‘must act now’ with cocaine-specific deaths eight times higher than in 2010

Cocaine has overtaken heroin as the biggest cause of drug deaths in England and Wales, figures from the Office for National Statistics show.

The government “must act now to reverse this deadly trend”, charities have said, with 1,233 deaths caused by cocaine last year.

Continue reading...
title: Cocaine overtakes heroin as leading cause of drug deaths in England and Wales

author: Jessica Salter
description:
Fancy stationery, cashmere knits and truly beautiful ceramics … we’ve handpicked 61 thoughtful gifts to spoil the mother figure in your life for Christmas 2026

• Don’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

A lot of stuff gets marketed as perfect for mums. But be careful, she really doesn’t want a kegel exerciser in her stocking, nor anything that makes washing up easier, unless you just do it instead of her. Also, beware of joke presents – they end up in the bin.

The perfect present for a mother figure of any age – be that a cherished aunt or beloved granny – is, I think, something either personal (which is where personalisation options can be useful) or an elevated version of something
title: The best Christmas gifts in the UK for mums, grannies, aunties and friends

author: Adrian Chiles
description:
You are shunted into side streets, crawling along, united with your fellow drivers in wordless despair. Last week, at 2am, my spirit broke

The worst three words in the transport lexicon are often said to be “rail”, “replacement” and “bus”, in that order. But there’s worse. “Motorway closed” is worse. At least with rail replacement buses you get fair warning, on booking apps and whatnot. You can resolve to embrace the pain or, more likely, abandon the journey. Motorway closures, in the dead of night, invariably come as a nasty surprise.

Waze, Google Maps, Apple Maps, etc can reliably get you from a car park in Penzance to a cul-de-sac in East Kilbride, but often can’t tell the difference between an open motorway and a shut motorway in the middle of the night. Football fans know all about this. You travel across the country for an evening match, and you lose. The prospect of a long drive home blackens your mood further, but as you slope away from the ground you cling to o
title: The worst two words in the dead of night? ‘Motorway closed’ | Adrian Chiles

author: Eddy Frankel
description:
A show of smart forgeries by Sturtevant will test your critical eye. Elsewhere, there’s a chance to dissect America’s cultural corpse and enter a terrifying immersive painting of Mexico

Cady Noland’s US is a violent, celebrity obsessed, consumerist police state. In this small show of big, stark, awkwardly cropped and blurry black and white images and minimal sculptures, the influential American iconoclast is dissecting her country’s cultural detritus, and leaving its splayed corpse on display.

Continue reading...
title: Can you tell a real Warhol from a fake? Four art exhibitions to see for free

author: Jess Cartner-Morley
description:
Black feels like a no-brainer for boots, handbags or coats - but if you swap it for brown, the same outfit looks more considered

There are a bunch of names being thrown around for the colour fashion wants us to wear this season. Espresso. Chestnut. Cacao. Ganache. Coffee bean. Truffle. Mocha. Caramel. Hazelnut. Nobody seems terribly keen to call it brown. Brown has never been the sexiest word in the paintbox. Red is passion. Black is chic. Pink is romance. Blue is serenity. Brown is the colour of wheelie bins. Except that right now, brown – specifically the deep, glossy, edible-looking chocolate end of the spectrum – is probably the chicest colour you can wear.

It is probably not incidental that we so often describe it in terms of what we eat or drink. When Pantone named Mocha Mousse its colour of 2025, it linked brown’s popularity to the “food
title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: chocolate, mocha, cacao … whatever you call it, brown is autumn’s chicest shade

author: Phillip Inman
description:
Purchasing manager’s index at eight-month high, bolstered by spending on AI as firms regain momentum lost to Iran war

  • Business live – latest updates

The Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates on Thursday after a closely watched survey showed growth across the UK’s services sector leapt last month to an eight-month high, bolstered by spending on artificial intelligence.

S&P Global’s survey of the services sector in October showed businesses regained much of the momentum they lost after the start of the Iran war, but also felt the impact of a renewed spurt of input price inflation, which accelerated to a five-month high.
title: UK interest rates increase expected after services sector activity accelerates

author: André Spicer
description:
A new proposal for openness about pay could have unexpected downsides – if workers become demotivated, resentful and more likely to quit

Would you like to know what your colleagues are paid? If the Equality and Human Rights Commission gets its way, you will be able to find out. Under its proposals, workers will be able to request detailed information about the pay, bonuses and other perks received by their co-workers. The government agency argues that if we increase pay transparency, we can also reduce the pay gap between men and women. But countries that have tried this model have discovered that there are downsides to it too.

The gap between men’s and women’s pay had started to close when equal pay legislation was introduced in Britain in the 1970s, a
title: Want to know what all your co-workers earn? Be careful what you wish for | André Spicer

author: Tom Hunt
description:
Mixed-up pasta bits and stale crisps combine with beans and cheese ends to make a fun and nutritious meal

The Northern Pasta Co’s new cookbook, Pasta For The People, includes a recipe for my pasta mista fritatta, a super-easy, child-friendly way to use up the end of a bag of pasta; it’s also a great vehicle for giving kids a filling, protein-rich meal with a portion of veg. I’ve come up with today’s dish in much the same spirit, and it ticks all the boxes.

Continue reading...
title: How to turn pasta odds and ends into a winning bake – recipe | Waste not

author: Tom Garry
description:
WSL’s second-highest goalscorer is likened to England legend for her crossing and has earned France call-up

At the conclusion of Birmingham’s warm-up, the players quietly and carefully placed their footballs into a draw-string bag. All except one, Océane Hurtré, who nonchalantly chipped hers straight into the bag from about 15 yards. It was an innocuous moment that might have escaped most onlookers at Hednesford Town’s Keys Park but it demonstrated the swagger with which she is playing.

To observe the 22-year-old warming up before last week’s 1-1 League Cup draw at Aston Villa was to witness a player making skills look easy, taking one touch where others took two and pulling off no-look passes. She is backing up that panache in the Women’s Super League, as the joint-second-highest goalscorer with six from the promoted side’s opening eight matches. Only Khadija Shaw has scored more.
title: ‘She can do what Beckham did’: Océane Hurtré making waves at Birmingham

author: Guardian community team
description:
We would like to hear from young people in the north of England about their experiences of looking for work

About 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds in the UK are not in employment, education or training (Neet), according to a report published in May, which warned that the figure could rise to 1.25 million by the early 2030s without urgent government action.

We are particularly keen to hear from young people living in northern England who are not currently in work or education, or who have been struggling to find a job.

Continue reading...
title: Tell us: are you a young person in northern England struggling to find work?

author: Andrew Lawrence
description:
There are small pleasures to be had in this straightforward retelling of the boxing champ’s life but there’s not much most viewers haven’t seen before

The Greatest is a new limited series that repackages the life of Muhammad Ali for generations born too late to remember when the sporting icon was the world’s most famous man, or too lazy to seek out one of the many books written about his boxing rise, his exile from the sport for refusing the draft, his improbable late-career comeback and his steely resilience in the face of a seismic Parkinson’s diagnosis. That this TV adaptation comes from Amazon is both a stroke of vertical integration and an indictment of a viewing public whose patience for source material wears thinner with every scroll.

The Prime Video drama says it’s base
title: The Greatest review – Amazon’s sturdy Muhammad Ali series is a tale told too many times

author: Mike McCahill
description:
A cast including Richard E Grant, Celia Imrie, Kiell Smith-Bynoe and Nigel Planer warm up a formulaic narrative about a imperilled retirement community

The annual drive to expand the festive film canon begins unseasonably early with a modest, sentimentally inclined Britpic that opens like a penny-pinching John Lewis ad; thankfully, it improves from there. The titular Mr Flint (John Bradley) is a Napoleonic history buff whose animus towards late December dates from seeing his (French) mother drop dead amid the Christmas decorations; now he spends the holidays cavilling at carollers and insisting that the icy pavements of his native York come with health-and-safety warnings. This very much not being the kind of film to confirm a fellow in such beliefs, Aubrey is instead nudged towards a developer-targeted retirement community planning one last theatre production; and when the residents choose A Christmas Carol, it all but closes the book on where this film is heading.

The
title: Merry Christmas Aubrey Flint review – Dickensian festive Britpic decorated by selection box of familiar faces

author: Anonymous
description:
Harsher settlement rules wouldn’t have stopped me fleeing hell in Syria to reach the UK. Now I’m here, they will just pile trauma on top of trauma

I am a refugee and I am in shock at the home secretary’s announcement that people like me will now have to wait up to 30 years before they can apply for settlement in the UK – a sixfold increase on the current time period.

It feels like a pile-on at a time when asylum seekers and refugees are already facing a barrage of hostility in this country. Even before the announcement, refugees felt under siege. With the withdrawal of the right to ever become citizens for those of us who have “made a dangerous journey” and with frequent reviews of our refugee status to check if we are s
title: These cruel new plans to ‘stop the boats’ show the government completely misunderstands refugees like me | Anonymous

author: Anna Tims
description:
Access to our £37,000 deposit in a savings account is restricted after a ‘routine security review’

My wife’s Revolut account was frozen in what it calls a “routine security review” over a week ago. Nothing has been requested from her – no documents, the source of funds, or ID – yet, as a result, our house deposit of £37,000 in a joint savings account is also restricted.

We’re approaching the completion of our property purchase and have given notice on our rental home. Direct debits are bouncing and we’re concerned about our credit records.

Continue reading...
title: Our house purchase is at risk from a frozen Revolut account

author: Rachel Dixon
description:
With its secluded orchard location, private sauna and hot tub, this off-grid cabin is the perfect place to kickback, with beaches and pubs just a short stroll away

As we walked through the orchard to our cabin at dusk, shadowy figures emerged from the mist. We stood stock-still and held our breath. Most of them saw us and fled, but one held its ground, unwilling to relinquish its stolen goods. Muntjac have clearly developed quite a taste for windfall apples.

My boyfriend and I left the little deer to dinner and walked on to the quince orchard, where our cabin waited in the far corner. This is the sixth Red Cabin to open in the UK. The first was on a sheep farm in Kent; others followed on farms and vineyards in south and east England. Ours was on Drove Orchards on the edge of the village of Thornham, on the north Norfolk coast.
title: ‘Overlooked only by trees’: a calming autumn cabin stay in north Norfolk

author: Phil Harrison, Ali Catterall, Jack Seale, Hollie Richardson and Priya Elan
description:
Prepare yourself for the duo’s all-female reimagining of Only Fools and Horses. Plus: Celebrity Race Across the World reaches Borneo. Here’s what to watch this evening

10pm, BBC Two

Continue reading...
title: TV tonight: the final episode of gloriously daft sketch show Ellie & Natasia

author: Alex Lawson and agencies
description:
House prices forecast to fall by 1.5% next year as Middle East war keeps mortgage rates higher for longer

Britain’s sluggish housing market is not expected to recover until 2028 as higher mortgage rates linked to the war in the Middle East deter buyers and weigh on prices.

The property firm Savills said average house prices were expected to drift lower during the rest of 2026 and fall by 1.5% in 2027, as the prolonged conflict undermines buyers’ confidence and keeps mortgage rates higher for longer.

Continue reading...
title: Britain’s housing market unlikely to recover until 2028, says Savills

author: Jonathan Jones
description:
V&A, London
Treasures from the two world-defining cultures that somehow coexisted in one mighty city keep on dazzling in this gorgeous, unmissable show

Two empires compete to bewitch you in this exhibition that offers a double bubble of beauty. It collides the Byzantine empire, whose capital Constantinople was officially inaugurated on 11 May AD330, with the Ottoman Turks who conquered this great city in 1453 and turned it into Istanbul. The combined glories of two lost worlds – the Ottoman empire was dissolved in 1922 – beget an utterly enrapturing blockbuster. I lost all track of time in this dream city of gold and ivory.

Even the human form is magically transfigured here into mineral and metal. The martyred abbess St Eudokia becomes a Byzantine icon of marble inlaid with coloured glass, wearing a crown of precious stones and an exquisite dress patterned with diamonds and decorated with pearls and emeralds. It is a masterpiece o
title: Constantinople to Istanbul review – you won’t want to leave this lavish celebration of double imperial splendour

author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
description:
Report says cost of maintenance could soon reach £2m a week, including 24-hour patrols to avert fire risk

The Palace of Westminster will be at risk of a Notre Dame-style fire or a similar catastrophic event if MPs do not tackle the issue of funding refurbishments, a parliamentary committee has said.

Decisions about how and when to begin a full restoration of the building, which is Grade I-listed and a Unesco world heritage site, have been repeatedly delayed amid disagreement over how it should be done and spiralling costs.

Continue reading...
title: Houses of Parliament at risk of ‘Notre Dame-style fire’ as renovation costs rise
